title: Janaka, the busy king
hookLine: a sage's son is sent to learn stillness from a king with a kingdom to run
carry: karma yoga: busy hands, a still self

lines: A KING WITH A KINGDOM TO RUN.
cards: Where would you go to learn stillness? A cave, a forest, a hermit's hut. In the Mahabharata, the sage Vyasa has a son, Shuka, who already seems made for the forest.
But when it's time to finish Shuka's learning, his father sends him somewhere else: to a palace, to King Janaka of Mithila, a man with a whole kingdom to run.

teach.b: In the Mahabharata's telling, Shuka walks to Mithila and is kept waiting at the gate, and sits there unbothered.
Then he's led inside, into gardens full of music and attendants and every comfort, and sits there just as still. Only then does the king come out to teach him.
The stillness Shuka found in the forest, Janaka keeps in a palace, between petitions and taxes.

teach.h: IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.
teach.b: The Mahabharata gives Janaka a saying Hindus still repeat: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. Not that he wouldn't fight the fire; a king would. But who he is doesn't burn with it.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points to him by name: by action alone, Janaka and others reached perfection.

teach.h: A DESERT IN THE BUSY STREET.
teach.b: That's the ideal of karma yoga, and Vivekananda drew it in his own picture: the ideal person finds intense activity in the deepest silence, and in the middle of intense activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert.
Such a person, he says, walks the busy streets of a big city as calm as if in a cave. That's the Hindu householder's path: you don't have to leave the family, the job or the city to walk toward God.
Serving each person as God, offering the fruit of the work, choosing what you dwell on, this whole week has been one skill: stay in the middle of the world without being swept off by it.
So the student, the parent with three jobs, the nurse on a double shift, each has Janaka's kingdom, and Janaka's still place. Which leaves a question: how do you actually find that quiet?
Karma Yoga mostly answers with work. Vivekananda has another book that goes straight at the mind, and that's tomorrow.

how: Hindus hold up King Janaka as the model of a householder who lived the spiritual life in the middle of work, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

o: the yoga of work, calm inside even the busiest day
keeping busy so the mind never has to be still
a desert retreat made once in a whole lifetime

games.q: the busy king — tap the pairs.
p: Vyasa's son, sent to learn from a king
the desert's silence in intense activity

s: Vyasa sent Shuka to a hermit in a cave for his last lesson
he sent him to King Janaka, a man with a kingdom to run.
in the Gita, Krishna names Janaka as someone who reached perfection by action
by action alone, Janaka and others reached it.
Vivekananda's ideal is to leave busy places for the quiet of the desert
his ideal finds the desert's silence in the middle of intense activity.

games.q: your day is loud and full, like a king's. what would Janaka do?
o: do the work fully, and keep the still place inside.
work faster to finish the noise sooner.
games.why: Janaka ran a kingdom and stayed still within: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. karma yoga doesn't escape the noise; it finds the desert in the middle of it.

practice: For the first part of the sit, let the world in: every sound, every itch, every thought about what's next, without pushing any of it away.
Then, changing nothing outside, look for the still place underneath, the part of you noticing the noise that isn't noisy itself, and rest there while the sounds go on.
If you pray, you can hold that stillness in a prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, Janaka's way: busy hands, and a still self in the middle of the busiest street.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga, busy hands, a still self. Janaka's way, and a whole week in one picture. Day nine hundred forty-five, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Shuka's visit to King Janaka; Janaka's saying that if Mithila burns, nothing of his burns)
Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 1, Karma in Its Effect on Character (the ideal man: silence in activity, activity in silence)
sources.work: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (paraphrased)
